explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The writer says the law is “…only a shadow of the good things to come, not the realities themselves.” A shadow of a cookie on the counter tells you a cookie is near, but nobody ever got fed by the shadow. The law points ahead to something better.

Close, but this shadow doesn't point backward. It points forward. The writer says the law is a shadow of “…the good things to come…” So the shadow is leaning toward what's ahead, not hanging around in the old days.

I get why you went there, friend, because sins come up a lot in this passage. But the writer says the law is a shadow of “…the good things to come…” Sins show up in the very next verses, as something the sacrifices keep reminding people of. The shadow itself is aimed at what's coming.

Careful, friend, this one has a twist at the end. The writer says the law can never, by the same sacrifices offered year after year, “…make perfect those who draw near to worship.” So the sacrifices do not make the worshipers perfect. The card flipped the writer's point on its head.

You caught the twist, baker. The writer says the law can never, by the same sacrifices offered year after year, “…make perfect those who draw near to worship.” The law is a shadow, and a shadow can't do the job of the real thing. Year after year the same sacrifices keep coming, and they still can't make anyone perfect.

Right on the money. The writer asks, “If it could, would not the offerings have ceased?” Think about it. When a job is truly finished, you quit doing it. The offerings kept going, and that tells us they couldn't do the job.

Doubled? Friend, that's the opposite direction. The writer asks, “If it could, would not the offerings have ceased?” If those sacrifices had made the worshipers perfect, nobody would need to keep offering them. Less, not more.

Cost never comes up here, baker. The writer asks, “If it could, would not the offerings have ceased?” His point is about the offerings stopping. If they had truly cleansed the worshipers once for all, there'd be no more offerings to price.

Yes, baker. The writer says, “Instead, those sacrifices are an annual reminder of sins…” Every year they brought the sins back to mind instead of ending them. I know a little about being reminded of things, because the junk drawer taught me what a pile of old receipts feels like.

Nice hope, friend, but a pardon is not what the writer says those sacrifices gave. He calls them “…an annual reminder of sins…” A reminder just points at the sin again. The forgiveness comes later in the passage, when the Lord says, “Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more.” (Hebrews 10:17)

Removal is exactly what the writer says those sacrifices could not do. He says it is “…impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.” So the word he lands on for them is “reminder,” not removal. The sin was still there, and the sacrifices kept pointing at it.

You've got it, baker. When Christ came into the world, He said, “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire…” (Hebrews 10:5) He is speaking to God here, and the writer says they're words from Psalm 40. That's a quiet, serious line, so I'll just let it sit.

Daily offerings do show up in this passage, but not in Christ's words. The writer says priests offer the same sacrifices day after day (Hebrews 10:11). What Christ says to God is, “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire…” (Hebrews 10:5) So He is not asking for more of them.

Not in Christ's words, friend. He says to God, “Sacrifice and offering You did not desire…” and that God took no delight in burnt offerings and sin offerings (Hebrews 10:5-6). Then the writer says He “…takes away the first to establish the second.” (Hebrews 10:9) That doesn't sound like forever for the first.

That's the one, baker. Christ says, “Here I am, I have come to do Your will.” (Hebrews 10:9) He also says it is written about Him in the scroll. I like a mission with a clear job description, and this one is the clearest there is.

No temple building in these words, friend. What Christ says is, “Here I am, I have come to do Your will.” (Hebrews 10:9) The passage never has Him mention a construction project. He has come to do God's will, plain and simple.

Nope, the priests aren't what Christ is talking about here. He says, “Here I am, I have come to do Your will.” (Hebrews 10:9) The writer does talk about priests, though. He says they stand day after day offering the same sacrifices, while Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for all time (Hebrews 10:11-12).

True, baker. After replaying Christ's words, the writer adds a note in parentheses: “(although they are offered according to the law).” So he's telling us the sacrifices were offered according to the law, even though God did not desire them. A little side note, and it matters.

This one is actually true, friend. The writer replays Christ's words about sacrifices and offerings God did not desire. Then he adds a note: “(although they are offered according to the law).” I know, I got a little suspicious of that note too.

Once, baker. The writer says we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ “once for all.” One time, and it covers everything. I've baked a lot of batches, and I'd love a batch that only needed to be done once.

Yearly is the old way, friend. The writer says those earlier sacrifices were offered year after year, an annual reminder of sins (Hebrews 10:1, 3). But the sacrifice of Jesus Christ's body was “once for all.” No annual schedule needed.

Daily belongs to the priests, baker. The writer says every priest stands day after day to offer again and again the same sacrifices (Hebrews 10:11). The sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ was “once for all.” No repeats, no daily rounds.

explanations.answer: He sat down at God's right hand
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The writer says that when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, “He sat down at the right hand of God.” Compare that to the priests who stand day after day. When the work is truly finished, you sit down. I wish I could do that after one batch, but the ovens keep calling.

explanations.answer: He went back into the temple
explanations.explanation: Back into the temple is where the priests keep going, friend, standing and offering the same sacrifices again and again (Hebrews 10:11). But this Priest offered one sacrifice for all time, and then “He sat down at the right hand of God.” No return trip needed.

explanations.answer: He went out into the wilderness
explanations.explanation: The wilderness isn't in this verse, baker. The writer says that after offering one sacrifice for sins for all time, Jesus “sat down at the right hand of God.” It's a seat, not a trek. And that's a very different picture from a priest standing day after day.

True, baker. The writer says, “Since that time, He waits for His enemies to be made a footstool for His feet.” So after sitting down at God's right hand, Jesus waits. Waiting is something I know a bit about from my years in the dark, but this is a very different kind of waiting.

This one is true, friend. The writer says, “Since that time, He waits for His enemies to be made a footstool for His feet.” That's after Jesus sat down at the right hand of God. So the card is right, even if it looks like a trick.

Perfect, baker. The writer says, “…by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified.” One offering, and it lasts for all time. That's a lot more staying power than any cookie I've ever pulled out of the oven.

Wise sounds nice, friend, but it's not what the writer says. He says that by a single offering Jesus “…has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified.” Perfect is the word, and it's for all time. A single offering does all of that.

Strong is a fine word, baker, but the writer uses a different one. He says that by a single offering Jesus “…has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified.” So it's perfect for all time, and it comes from one single offering.

Yes, baker. The Lord says, “I will put My laws in their hearts and inscribe them on their minds.” The writer says these words come from the Holy Spirit's testimony. The laws go inside, to the heart and the mind.

Stone tablets aren't in what the Lord says here, friend. He says, “I will put My laws in their hearts and inscribe them on their minds.” The place is inside the people, in their hearts and minds. It's a covenant that gets written somewhere I can't stamp.

Doors are a creative guess, baker, but the Lord names a different place. He says, “I will put My laws in their hearts and inscribe them on their minds.” The writing goes on the people themselves, not on a building.

Careful, friend, that's the opposite of what the Lord says. He says, “Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more.” Yearly remembering was the old way, when the sacrifices were “an annual reminder of sins.” (Hebrews 10:3) Under this covenant, the Lord says He remembers them no more.

Right, baker. The Lord says, “Their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more.” That is a big change from the sacrifices that served as “an annual reminder of sins.” (Hebrews 10:3) Not remembered, not even once a year.

That's the one, baker. The writer says, “And where these have been forgiven, an offering for sin is no longer needed.” When sins are forgiven, there's nothing left to offer for them. That ties it all together, and I'm happy to let it be the last word.

A feast is not what the writer says is no longer needed, friend. He says, “And where these have been forgiven, an offering for sin is no longer needed.” His whole point is about offerings for sin. Feasts are not part of this passage.

Fasting isn't in this passage, baker. The writer says, “And where these have been forgiven, an offering for sin is no longer needed.” Once sins are forgiven, an offering for sin has no more work to do. The writer says nothing here about a day of fasting.
